description: Five computer engineering students from Düzce University. Our skills: computer vision (YOLO), embedded systems (Jetson, ROS2), backend (FastAPI, Docker) and UAV/aerospace project work. We want to build a low-cost Earth-observation tool with NASA satellite data that solves a real problem and can be validated in 48 hours. Looking for: remote sensing/GIS (GeoPandas, Rasterio), data science/ML, frontend/mapping (React, Leaflet), and presentation/design skills.
summary:
Mars Space Vision is an EVA planning and monitoring tool that answers the first question of any walk on Mars: can I get there and safely come back? Built on real NASA and USGS data for Gale Crater (HiRISE imagery, the Gale elevation model and Mars Odyssey THEMIS infrared via Mars Trek), it does not just draw one route. For every map cell it computes outbound and return time under directional suit slope limits, oxygen and battery reserves, and shows the whole area an astronaut can reach and still return from. During a simulated EVA this return range shrinks live, a delay triggers the fastest way home, and a solar storm drill finds nearby terrain cover.

Our key finding: maps can be dangerously optimistic. When the same terrain is coarsened to 500 m, 59% of the area marked safe is not actually safe; on flat plains the error is 0%. Much of Mars is mapped at this scale, so data resolution itself is a safety risk.

details:
What it does
Mars Space Vision is an EVA planning and live-monitoring tool for astronauts on Mars. It answers one question: can I get there and safely come back? Instead of drawing a single route, it computes the whole area an astronaut can reach and still return from with the remaining oxygen and battery reserve, called the return envelope.

How it works
We use real NASA and USGS data for Gale Crater: HiRISE imagery, the USGS Gale merged elevation model (1 m, resampled to 5–10 m walking grids) and Mars Odyssey THEMIS infrared via NASA Mars Trek. From the elevation model we compute slope, then run a forward search from the habitat and a reverse search back to it. A cell is safe only if outbound + return time stays within the reserve. Costs are directional: uphill, downhill and cross-slope have separate spacesuit limits (18°, 12°, 10°), so the way back is planned separately from the way out. During a simulated EVA, the return range shrinks live. A delay triggers the fastest way home, and a solar particle event drill finds nearby terrain cover. Radio line of sight to base and Mars24-based sunlight are also shown.

Key finding
We measured how much map resolution hides risk. When the same terrain is coarsened to 500 m, 59% of the area that looks safe is not actually safe, while flat plains show 0% error. Much of Mars is mapped at this scale, so data resolution itself is a safety factor.

Benefits and impact
Crews on Mars cannot wait for Earth: communication is delayed by up to 22 minutes. Our tool supports habitat crews, mission planners, astronaut training and Mars analog missions. It extends the Apollo “walkback” rule, which assumed constant walking speed, to real terrain and slope. The same engine works with any elevation model, including the Moon for Artemis.

Tools
TypeScript, React and Vite for the web app; Leaflet for 2D maps; Three.js for 3D terrain and the helmet camera view; Python scripts for data preparation; automated unit and browser tests. No server, no database, no special hardware: it runs offline in any modern browser and uses only free, open data.

Creativity
Most planners ask “what is the best route?” We ask “how far can I go and still return, and how much can I trust this map?” Turning the data’s own uncertainty into a measurable safety result is our main creative contribution.

Factors we considered
Astronaut safety reserves, asymmetric slope effort, suit limits, communication loss, lighting, radiation events, and honesty: oxygen rates are labeled as training assumptions, the walking model comes from Earth data, and the tool is a decision-support prototype, not a certified safety system.
